name: Result / Railway Pattern
intent: Represent success or predictable failure as an explicit value rather than throwing runtime exceptions
modern_alternative: Result<T, E> type, Either monad, Go (value, error) tuple
when_to_use: Domain operations with anticipated failure modes (validation, user not found, rate limited)
anti_patterns: Throwing exceptions for expected business logic branches, returning null on error

name: Typestate Pattern
intent: Encode object state transitions into the type system to make invalid states unrepresentable at compile time
modern_alternative: Phantom types, builder with generic state markers, TypeScript discriminated unions
when_to_use: Multi-step workflows where operations are only valid in specific phases (Draft -> Submitted -> Paid)
anti_patterns: Runtime enum checks throwing IllegalStateException, boolean state flags like isSubmitted

name: Functional Options
intent: Provide clean, extensible configuration for structs or classes with defaults without constructor explosion
modern_alternative: Variadic WithOption closures (Go), fluent Builder (TS/Rust), keyword args with defaults (Python)
when_to_use: Constructors with >3 optional parameters or configurations that may evolve over time
anti_patterns: Overloaded constructors (NewClient1, NewClient2), passing structs with 15 nil fields

name: Type-Safe Fluent Builder
intent: Construct complex objects step-by-step, enforcing required parameters at compile time
modern_alternative: Fluent builder returning state-carrying generic types or validated build() method
when_to_use: Constructing complex immutable domain aggregates with many required and optional fields
anti_patterns: Telescoping constructors with 8 arguments, partially initialized mutable objects

name: Factory Method / Smart Constructor
intent: Encapsulate object creation logic and validation inside static functions rather than raw constructors
modern_alternative: Static create() or parse() methods returning Result<T, E> or validated instance
when_to_use: Enforcing validation invariants upon creation (e.g. Email.create('a@b.com'))
anti_patterns: Public raw constructors that allow creating invalid or unvalidated domain objects

name: Specification Pattern
intent: Encapsulate business rules into reusable, combinable Boolean predicates (And, Or, Not)
modern_alternative: Higher-order predicate functions, type-safe expression objects
when_to_use: Complex search filters, validation rules applied across multiple domain operations
anti_patterns: God-validator classes with 500-line if-else chains, duplicating rule logic in UI and backend

name: Value Object / Branded Type
intent: Represent domain concepts defined by their attributes rather than identity; enforce immutability and self-validation
modern_alternative: Readonly dataclasses (Python), readonly structs (Rust/C#), branded types / nominal tags (TS)
when_to_use: Domain primitives with validation invariants (Email, Money, Currency, OrderQuantity, GeoPoint)
anti_patterns: Primitive obsession (passing raw string/number everywhere), mutable value objects

name: Strategy Pattern
intent: Define a family of algorithms, encapsulate each one, and make them interchangeable at runtime
modern_alternative: First-class functions / closures, typed protocols, function mapping table
when_to_use: Multiple payment processors, serialization formats, pricing calculation engines
anti_patterns: Giant switch/case statements, deep inheritance hierarchies for algorithm variants

name: Decorator / Middleware Chain
intent: Attach additional responsibilities (logging, auth, metrics, tracing) dynamically and transparently
modern_alternative: Composable handler wrappers, async middleware pipelines (koa/axum/actix style)
when_to_use: Cross-cutting concerns on HTTP requests, command handlers, or event consumers
anti_patterns: Hardcoding auth/logging inside every domain service, circular decorator dependencies

name: Adapter Pattern
intent: Convert the interface of an external library or legacy class into an interface expected by domain clients
modern_alternative: Thin wrapper class or translation function implementing a domain port
when_to_use: Decoupling application logic from third-party SDK signatures or disparate vendor APIs
anti_patterns: Leaking third-party SDK types across the adapter boundary into domain logic

name: Observer / Typed Signal
intent: Define a one-to-many dependency between objects so that when one object changes state, dependents are notified
modern_alternative: Typed EventEmitter, in-process Channel, Observable, Rx streams
when_to_use: Decoupling state changes in a domain service from side effects (UI updates, cache invalidation)
anti_patterns: Global untyped string-based event emitters, memory leaks from unremoved event listeners

name: Command Pattern
intent: Encapsulate a request as an object, enabling parameterization of clients with queues, logs, and undo operations
modern_alternative: Command structs/classes with execute() and optional undo(), async job payloads
when_to_use: Transactional task scheduling, undo/redo stacks, asynchronous task execution queues
anti_patterns: God command objects that contain entire domain workflows instead of delegating to domain services

name: Discriminated Union / Tagged Union
intent: Represent a value that could be one of several distinct variants with an explicit discriminator tag
modern_alternative: Tagged union (Rust enum, Swift enum, TS type union with kind/type tag, Python Union with Literal)
when_to_use: Domain events, state machine representations, AST nodes, heterogeneous message payloads
anti_patterns: Using instanceof or typeof checks without compiler exhaustiveness checking, untagged any

name: Constructor Dependency Injection
intent: Pass all required dependencies explicitly through the constructor or factory function
modern_alternative: Pure parameter passing, manual composition root (wire.go, main.ts)
when_to_use: All service classes and business logic components needing testability and modularity
anti_patterns: Global ServiceLocator.get(), importing singleton instances directly, newing dependencies inside methods
